title: Houthis Kill 30+ Yemeni Troops, Trump Targets Birthright Citizenship and Chip Supply Chains, Ceuta Crisis Deepens
subhead: Houthi missile strikes on Yemeni government camps mark the deadliest escalation since the group's maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia began, while Trump pushes new executive orders on birthright citizenship and polysilicon tariffs on China, and thousands of migrants remain stranded in Ceuta with new crossings reportedly being organized online.

sections.heading: Houthi Strikes Kill Dozens in Yemen as Maritime Embargo Escalates
sections.body:
Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones at Yemeni government military camps in the central provinces of Marib and Hadramawt on Thursday, killing at least 30 troops and wounding many more, according to Yemen's defence ministry. Military sources cited by AFP put the death toll as high as 58, with other reports exceeding 40.

The Houthis claimed they targeted 'large Saudi military build-ups' preparing for an offensive. A Saudi-led coalition spokesperson said 11 civilians, including a four-year-old child, were wounded in a separate Houthi strike on the Saudi border region of Najran. Yemen's government denounced the attacks as 'treacherous' and vowed to respond.

The strikes come two weeks after the Houthis announced a 'maritime embargo' against Saudi Arabia on July 20, following what they described as a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory. Saudi Arabia has responded with strikes on Houthi positions and formed a new naval coalition to protect Red Sea shipping; 43 countries attended the coalition's founding meeting on Thursday, with the new commander stressing it was 'purely defensive in nature.'

The UN called on all parties to 'exercise restraint,' warning that renewed fighting risks reversing hard-won gains in reducing violence since the 2022 ceasefire.
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthi escalation from maritime attacks on shipping to mass-casualty strikes on ground forces signals the Yemen conflict is entering a more violent phase, with the Saudi-led naval coalition adding a new dimension to an already complex Red Sea security picture.

sections.heading: Trump Signs New Executive Orders Targeting Birthright Citizenship
sections.body:
President Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday seeking to limit birthright citizenship, weeks after the Supreme Court ruled his earlier attempt to restrict the practice unconstitutional.

The new orders are narrower than Trump's initial effort, which sought to deny citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants and temporary visa holders. One order expands the existing exception for children of foreign diplomats and 'invading forces' to also exclude children of alleged 'terrorists,' people deemed to be attempting to 'purchase' citizenship, and certain people born in US territories. The second order directs the secretaries of state and homeland security to halt so-called 'birth tourism.'

The move follows a June Supreme Court ruling, where six justices — including Chief Justice John Roberts, a conservative — rejected Trump's attempt to narrow the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause, calling it a 'dramatically revisionist view' with 'scant evidence.' Legal experts told Al Jazeera the new orders are also likely to be found unconstitutional. Constitutional law expert Kimberly Wehle said Trump appeared to be 'setting up a clash between himself and the authority of the United States Supreme Court' at a time when his poll numbers are slumping.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump is deliberately creating a constitutional confrontation with the judiciary over birthright citizenship, testing the limits of executive power on an issue central to his political brand despite a decisive Supreme Court rebuke just weeks ago.

sections.heading: Trump Imposes 15% Tariff on Polysilicon as US-China Tech Fight Deepens
sections.body:
Trump signed an executive order imposing a 15% tariff on imported polysilicon and related products, along with minimum import prices, citing a national security investigation into overseas production. The measures take effect in December.

Polysilicon is a critical material used in semiconductors and solar panels. China holds a near-monopoly on global production, and the US share has fallen from 50% in 2005 to less than 2% in 2024, according to Trump's order. The move is designed to protect US manufacturers like Hemlock Semiconductor and Wacker Chemie.

The Chinese embassy in Washington called the tariff a move that 'seriously disrupts' trade and accused Washington of 'abusing state power to go after Chinese businesses.' Beijing this week announced countermeasures including tighter drone export controls and a national security review of imported printers and copiers. Analysts cited by Chinese state media described the tariff as the latest escalation in Washington's effort to limit China's role in critical technology supply chains, following earlier restrictions on drones and humanoid robots.
sections.whyItMatters: The polysilicon tariff targets a material chokepoint where China dominates and the US has virtually no domestic capacity, signaling that the tech decoupling between the two economies is now reaching deep into foundational industrial inputs.

sections.heading: Ceuta Migrant Crisis Enters Second Week as 3,000-5,000 Remain
sections.body:
Between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in the Spanish territory of Ceuta after roughly 78,000 people crossed from Morocco by sea last week, Ceuta's mayor-president Juan Jesús Vivas told the European Parliament on Thursday. Vivas said 100 people died in the crossings and described the situation as an 'irreparable tragedy.'

Nearly 75,000 migrants have been returned to Morocco, but the situation has not returned to normal. Vivas said returning unaccompanied minors was 'basically impossible' because it requires their consent, and volunteer groups have registered 4,860 migrant children — double official estimates. Spain's interior ministry has allocated €25m to assist minors, but no children have been moved to mainland Spain so far.

The crisis has created a diplomatic rift within the EU: Italy suspended its Schengen arrangement with Spain, backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's Schengen membership to be temporarily suspended. EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said the EU was 'ready to do more' but had not received a further request for border guards from Spain. Meanwhile, Moroccan media report that fresh calls for another mass crossing attempt are circulating on social media.
sections.whyItMatters: The Ceuta crisis is testing the EU's Schengen system and exposing deep divisions over migration policy, while the prospect of renewed mass crossings threatens to turn a one-time crisis into a persistent security challenge on Europe's African border.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Oil Refineries 1,300km Inside Russia
sections.body:
Ukraine struck two oil refineries deep inside Russian territory overnight, with President Zelensky confirming attacks on the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Bashkortostan — roughly 1,300km from the Ukrainian border — and the Slavneft-Yanos refinery in Yaroslavl, nearly 700km inside Russia. Yaroslavl's governor said the Slavneft-Yanos refinery was on fire after what he called the 'largest enemy drone attack' on the region, with 93 drones shot down overnight and four people injured.

Zelensky said Ukrainian forces also hit 'two military patrol boats and shadow fleet vessels' in the Black Sea, referring to tankers Russia uses to export sanctioned oil. 'Russia must choose peace,' he said, adding the strikes were 'strengthening chances for diplomacy.'

On the receiving end, Russia said it intercepted or shot down 605 Ukrainian drones overnight and struck Ukrainian fuel, energy, and transport facilities. At least 11 people were killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine: three in Balakliya, two at a train station in Lozova, and five in Dnipropetrovsk region. The southern city of Kherson experienced a total blackout after a critical infrastructure hit, with internet connectivity dropping to 31% at its lowest.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's ability to strike refineries 1,300km into Russian territory demonstrates the continued reach of its drone program, while Russia's 605-drone barrage shows Moscow is matching the escalation — both sides are hitting energy infrastructure hard as the ground war stays static and diplomacy stalls.

sections.heading: US Munitions Shortage Denial Deepens as Trump Targets Leakers
sections.body:
President Trump denied reports of a US munitions shortage, posting on Truth Social that 'The U.S. has massive amounts of munitions, especially of certain types' and vowing to seek 'long term jail sentences' for those leaking information about stockpile levels.

His comments followed a CBS News report that the US has used much of its global stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the Iran conflict, and a Washington Post report that Trump confronted Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over a possible weapons shortfall. Trump called the Washington Post's reporting 'treasonous.'

CSIS estimates that by end of July, the US had between 759 and 827 Patriot missiles remaining — roughly one-third of the 2,330 available before the conflict began — and that approximately 60% of THAAD interceptor missiles have been expended. Hegseth has asked the Senate for $87bn in emergency funds to 'rapidly replenish equipment and munitions.' Trump also said that granting Ukraine's request for additional Patriot missiles would be a 'big step' but the two countries were 'still talking about it.'

Iran's Defence Minister Majid Ibn-e-Reza responded that 'each day, the signs of the enemy's diminishing capabilities become more apparent,' claiming Iran's indigenous weapons production gives it the ability to respond to 'any threat.'
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between official reassurances and independent assessments of US munitions levels is widening, with the administration treating stockpile leaks as a criminal matter rather than addressing the underlying depletion — a stance that affects not just the Iran conflict but also Ukraine's pending Patriot requests.

bottomLine: A day of escalation on multiple fronts: Houthi mass-casualty strikes on Yemeni government forces signal the Red Sea conflict is entering a deadlier phase, while Trump tests constitutional and trade boundaries with new birthright citizenship orders and polysilicon tariffs aimed at China. In Ceuta, thousands of migrants remain stranded as EU solidarity fractures over Schengen, and Ukraine demonstrated it can still hit Russian refineries 1,300km deep while absorbing a 600-drone Russian barrage. The US munitions debate shifted from substance to leak-pursuit, with Trump threatening jail for those revealing stockpile data as independent estimates show Patriot missile reserves down to a third of pre-war levels.
